    Jasper Plugin SDK 0.21.0

    Build the workstation you need.

    Jasper is a pluggable DevOps workstation: its SSH, SFTP and tunnels, credential vault, editor, file servers, project index, shell history and snippets are all plugins written against this SDK. This reference is the guide to writing your own and the complete API they use.

    • 12 SDK packages
    • 298 documented types
    • 12 capabilities
    • JDK only no dependencies

    Overview

    Jasper is a pluggable DevOps workstation for macOS, Linux and Windows. The application itself provides the workspace (windows, tabs, panes and tool windows), the terminal, the command palette, notifications, Settings, themes and looks. Most of what you use beyond that, from SSH sessions to the credential vault, ships as plugins written against this SDK, and a plugin you write uses the same API as the plugins Jasper ships with. Bundled plugins differ in a few rules: they need no capability review, only they can be off by default, they load in safe mode unless they provide a look, and they take precedence for the editor role and for a subcommand name two loading plugins declare.

    What a plugin can do

    • Commands and chromeActions that appear in the command palette and Settings › Keymap with default shortcuts, placed in menus, the toolbar, the status bar and the tool window stripe.
    • Tool windows and windowsDocked tool windows, windows of its own, dialogs, in-window overlays, popovers and document tabs in the workspace, all built from declarative views that Jasper draws.
    • TerminalsFind windows, tabs and panes, read what a pane runs, type into it, open local tabs, splits and programs, add environment variables to new shells, and follow 16 terminal events.
    • SessionsProvide a pane's session over its own connection, as Remote does for SSH: Jasper owns the pane, its banner and Reconnect.
    • Command paletteScopes of searchable rows with up to three verbs, an optional form step, recents, and a chip the user reaches by prefix or shortcut.
    • Notifications and activityNotification groups the user tunes in Settings, long-running activities and connection states shown on Desk Buddy.
    • SettingsTyped, validated settings in the plugin's own TOML file, read live, with a generated page in Settings › Tools or a page of the plugin's own.
    • Files and the editorPlaces in Jasper's file chooser, such as saved hosts, and the role of the editor Jasper opens files with.
    • Services for other pluginsInterfaces in an exported package that other plugins look up, as the Vault, Editor, Remote and Snippets plugins do.
    • The command linejasper <name> subcommands that run in the running Jasper and report an exit code.
    • Looks and themesA look (the presentation of the chrome and controls) and themes, declared as data in the manifest; any plugin can read which look Jasper runs with and compose for it.

    How a plugin runs

    A plugin is a folder of jars, one of which holds a plugin.toml manifest at its root. Jasper finds plugins once, when it starts, in three places: the plugins bundled in the application, the plugins folder in Jasper home, and the folder given with --plugin-dir. It checks each manifest, the SDK range, the plugin's dependencies and, for a plugin the user installed, the user's consent to its capabilities. It then loads each plugin in its own class loader, dependencies first, and calls its Plugin.start(PluginContext) on the UI thread with a PluginContext of its own. Jasper home is the folder that holds config.toml: ~/.config/jasper on macOS, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jasper (or ~/.config/jasper) on Linux and %APPDATA%\jasper on Windows, unless JASPER_HOME or the jasper.home Java property moves it; see configuration.

    A plugin's class loader sees the SDK, the Java runtime, the plugin's own jars and the packages that plugins it requires export; Jasper's own classes and libraries are not visible. Everything a plugin registers through its context is attributed to it and removed when it stops. Nothing loads or unloads while Jasper runs: installing, updating, enabling, disabling and removing a plugin take effect at the next launch.

    The SDK depends only on the JDK. A few signatures use AWT and Swing types: colours (java.awt.Color), a window's preferred size (java.awt.Dimension), a component's workspace opacity (java.awt.Component), custom content (javax.swing.JComponent) and content-tab shortcuts (javax.swing.KeyStroke). Plugins run on Java 25.

    The bundled plugins

    Each bundled plugin is an ordinary plugin on this SDK: it declares capabilities, requires other plugins and exports packages exactly as yours would, and each can be turned off in Settings › Plugins. Every one declares sdk = ">=0.21.0, <0.22".

    PluginIdCapabilitiesExportsRequires (optional)
    Remote: SSH, SFTP and tunnelsdev.jasper.remoteterminal.open, session.provide, terminal.observe, palette.contribute, files.sourcedev.jasper.remote.apiVault, Editor
    Credential Vaultdev.jasper.vaultpalette.contributedev.jasper.vault.api
    Editordev.jasper.editorpalette.contribute, terminal.environment, editor.provide, terminal.opendev.jasper.editor.api
    File Serverdev.jasper.fileservernetwork.listen, terminal.observe, palette.contribute, clipboard.readVault
    Project Indexdev.jasper.indexerterminal.observe, terminal.open, palette.contributeEditor, Remote
    Shell Historydev.jasper.historypalette.contribute, terminal.observe, terminal.injectSnippets
    Snippetsdev.jasper.snippetspalette.contribute, terminal.injectdev.jasper.snippets.api

    The Sample plugin is the SDK's end-to-end example and shows nothing until one of its demo_* settings is on. The exported packages and what they offer are described in Services and, for users of those plugins, in plugin APIs. The user's side of plugins (installing, reviewing, safe mode) is in plugins.

    Packages

    The SDK (jasper-sdk) is 12 packages under dev.jasper.sdk. The test kit (jasper-sdk-testkit) adds dev.jasper.sdk.testing, and the bundled plugins' exported packages complete the API reference below.

    PackageWhat it holds
    dev.jasper.sdkLeaf values shared by every SDK package: the SDK version, plugin identity, the capability names and the exception a gated call throws without one, the theme variant, the owner a dialog is parented to and the subscription returned by every registration.
    dev.jasper.sdk.pluginThe entry point a plugin implements and the context the runtime hands it.
    dev.jasper.sdk.activityLong-running work a plugin volunteers to show: begin an activity, report progress, end it once; or announce a connection, report its state as it changes and close it.
    dev.jasper.sdk.cliSubcommands of the jasper command.
    dev.jasper.sdk.eventsThe typed event bus: topics, subscription and publication, and the application's own topics.
    dev.jasper.sdk.filesPlaces plugins add to Jasper's file chooser, and what the chooser returns.
    dev.jasper.sdk.notificationsNotifications a plugin posts: groups the user tunes, plain-text specs with links, an optional cause that the host records as the plugin's incident, and handles that withdraw them.
    dev.jasper.sdk.paletteCommand-palette scopes contributed by plugins.
    dev.jasper.sdk.servicesPlugin-to-plugin services: a provider publishes an interface from one of its exported packages, a plugin that declares requires on the provider looks it up.
    dev.jasper.sdk.settingsPlugin settings: declarations of a plugin's settings, the typed handles that read, watch and save them, and the kinds that check their values.
    dev.jasper.sdk.terminalJasper's windows, tabs and panes as handles a plugin can query and drive, local tabs and splits it can open, sessions it can provide to a pane, the variables it can add to new local shells, and the jasper.terminal.* events.
    dev.jasper.sdk.uiWhat a plugin contributes to the application's chrome.
    dev.jasper.sdk.testingA headless, single-threaded stand-in for Jasper's plugin runtime, for plugin unit tests.
    dev.jasper.editor.apiThe Editor's exported API: open a local file, or a document another plugin reads and writes; make recent documents reopenable; answer Open in Editor… and offer a file source's places in Open in Editor… and Save As.
    dev.jasper.remote.apiRemote's exported API for other plugins: RemoteProjects, published with Services.publish, and its values.
    dev.jasper.snippets.apiWhat other plugins may use: the snippet service and its value.
    dev.jasper.vault.apiThe contract other plugins compile against: VaultApi and the lock state it reports, credentials with their kinds and descriptors, the anchored credential chooser's request and result, how a credential looks in a picker, and SSH key import sources and results.

    Using this reference

    The guide pages explain how the parts work together; the API reference after them documents every public type and member, grouped by package. Press / to search types and members. Worked examples taken from the Sample plugin are in plugin authoring, view compositions in plugin UI and icon rules in plugin icons.

    Quick start

    This page builds a complete plugin outside the Jasper repository: one command, in the Tools menu and the command palette, that copies a greeting to the clipboard. It compiles against the SDK 0.21.0 release jars with Gradle and any Java 25 JDK, has a unit test, runs in Jasper straight from the build folder and packages as a zip that users install. The same project is in the Jasper repository as docs/examples/external-plugin; Jasper's CI runs its check pluginZip against the jars sdkRelease makes.

    1. Get the SDK jars. Each Jasper GitHub release carries jasper-sdk-0.21.0.jar (with -sources and -javadoc jars) and jasper-sdk-testkit-0.21.0.jar (with -sources). Put the two main jars in your project's libs/ folder. From a Jasper checkout, ./gradlew sdkRelease builds the same jars into build/sdk-release/.
    2. Lay out the project. 
      hello-plugin/
  settings.gradle.kts
  build.gradle.kts
  libs/jasper-sdk-0.21.0.jar
  libs/jasper-sdk-testkit-0.21.0.jar
  src/main/resources/plugin.toml
  src/main/java/dev/example/hello/HelloPlugin.java
  src/test/java/dev/example/hello/HelloPluginTest.java
    3. Write the manifest, src/main/resources/plugin.toml, so it lands at the root of the plugin's jar. The id namespaces everything the plugin registers; the sdk range says which SDK versions it runs on (see Manifest and Versions). This plugin needs no capability. 
      id = "dev.example.hello"
name = "Hello"
version = "1.0.0"
entry = "dev.example.hello.HelloPlugin"
sdk = ">=0.21.0, <0.22"
description = "An example external plugin: a Tools menu command that copies a greeting."
vendor = "Example"
capabilities = []
exports = []
    4. Write the entry class. It is public with a public no-argument constructor, and implements Plugin. start runs on the UI thread: it registers an action, which every window's command palette lists, and places it in the Tools menu. Platform.copy(String) needs no capability. 
      package dev.example.hello;

import dev.jasper.sdk.plugin.Plugin;
import dev.jasper.sdk.plugin.PluginContext;
import dev.jasper.sdk.ui.ActionSpec;
import dev.jasper.sdk.ui.StandardMenu;
import java.util.List;

/** An example external plugin: one command, in the Tools menu and the palette, that copies a greeting. */
public final class HelloPlugin implements Plugin {
    static final String COPY = "dev.example.hello.copy";
    static final String GREETING = "Hello from an external Jasper plugin";

    @Override public void start(PluginContext context) {
        context.actions().register(ActionSpec.of(COPY, "Copy Greeting").withKeywords(List.of("hello", "greeting", "example")),
            invoked -> context.platform().copy(GREETING));
        context.menus().standard(StandardMenu.TOOLS).add(COPY);
    }
}
    5. Write the build. settings.gradle.kts names the project: 
      rootProject.name = "hello-plugin"
      build.gradle.kts compiles against the SDK jar as compileOnly, because Jasper supplies the SDK at run time, puts the SDK and test kit on the test classpath with JUnit and AssertJ, and adds the two packaging tasks. Libraries the plugin bundles go in implementation; they travel with it in the staged folder and the zip. 
      plugins { `java-library` }

val jasperSdkDir = file(providers.gradleProperty("jasperSdkDir").getOrElse("libs"))
val jasperSdkVersion = providers.gradleProperty("jasperSdkVersion").getOrElse("0.21.0")
fun jasperJar(name: String) = files(jasperSdkDir.resolve("$name-$jasperSdkVersion.jar"))

// Name the missing jar instead of failing later with "package dev.jasper.sdk... does not exist".
tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach {
    doFirst {
        for (name in listOf("jasper-sdk", "jasper-sdk-testkit")) {
            val jar = jasperSdkDir.resolve("$name-$jasperSdkVersion.jar")
            check(jar.isFile) {
                "Missing $jar: put the Jasper release's SDK jars in $jasperSdkDir, " +
                    "or pass -PjasperSdkDir=<folder> and -PjasperSdkVersion=<version>"
            }
        }
    }
}

/** The id and version come from plugin.toml, so the build keeps no second copy of either. */
val descriptor = file("src/main/resources/plugin.toml").readText()
fun field(name: String) = Regex("^$name\\s*=\\s*\"([^\"]+)\"", RegexOption.MULTILINE).find(descriptor)?.groupValues?.get(1)
    ?: error("plugin.toml has no $name")
val pluginId = field("id")
version = field("version")

repositories { mavenCentral() }

// Jasper runs plugins on Java 25; any Java 25 compiles them (Jasper itself needs the JetBrains Runtime only to run).
java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(25) } }

dependencies {
    compileOnly(jasperJar("jasper-sdk"))
    testImplementation(jasperJar("jasper-sdk"))
    testImplementation(jasperJar("jasper-sdk-testkit"))
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:6.1.3"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
    testImplementation("org.assertj:assertj-core:3.27.7")
}

tasks.jar { archiveBaseName.set(pluginId) }

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
    systemProperty("java.awt.headless", "true")
}

// What Jasper installs: the plugin jar beside the libraries it bundles (its runtime classpath).
//   stagePlugin -> build/plugin/<id>/                     (jasper --plugin-dir build/plugin/<id>)
//   pluginZip   -> build/distributions/<id>-<version>.zip (File > Manage Plugins... > Install from Zip...)
val pluginContents = files(tasks.jar, configurations.runtimeClasspath)

tasks.register<Sync>("stagePlugin") {
    description = "Stages $pluginId as a plugin directory for jasper --plugin-dir."
    group = "distribution"
    from(pluginContents)
    into(layout.buildDirectory.dir("plugin/$pluginId"))
}

tasks.register<Zip>("pluginZip") {
    description = "Zips $pluginId for File > Manage Plugins... > Install from Zip..."
    group = "distribution"
    from(pluginContents)
    archiveFileName.set("$pluginId-$version.zip")
    destinationDirectory.set(layout.buildDirectory.dir("distributions"))
}
    6. Test it. FakePluginHost runs the plugin headless, with the test thread as its UI thread (see Testing): 
      package dev.example.hello;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import dev.jasper.sdk.PluginInfo;
import dev.jasper.sdk.testing.FakePluginHost;
import java.util.Set;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class HelloPluginTest {
    @Test void theToolsCommandCopiesTheGreeting() {
        try (var host = new FakePluginHost()) {
            host.start(new PluginInfo("dev.example.hello", "Hello", "1.0.0", Set.of()), Set.of(), Set.of(), new HelloPlugin());
            assertThat(host.menu("TOOLS")).containsExactly("item:" + HelloPlugin.COPY);
            var window = host.addTerminalWindow();
            assertThat(host.invoke(HelloPlugin.COPY, window, null)).isTrue();
            assertThat(host.clipboard().copies()).containsExactly("copy|dev.example.hello|" + HelloPlugin.GREETING);
            assertThat(host.failures()).isEmpty();
        }
    }
}
    7. Build and run it in Jasper. The commands use a Gradle wrapper in the project (gradle wrapper makes one; Jasper's CI builds this example with Gradle 9.7.0). stagePlugin writes the plugin folder, the plugin jar beside the libraries it bundles; --plugin-dir starts a separate Jasper that loads it without a capability review: 
      ./gradlew check stagePlugin
jasper --plugin-dir build/plugin/dev.example.hello
      The jasper command must be on your PATH (Settings › Appearance & Behavior › System Settings › Command line installs it); otherwise start the application executable with the same option, for example /Applications/Jasper.app/Contents/MacOS/Jasper --plugin-dir build/plugin/dev.example.hello on macOS. See the command line. Copy Greeting is now in the Tools menu and the command palette, and Settings › Plugins lists Hello under Development. Stage again and restart that Jasper after each change: plugins load only at launch.
    8. Package and install it. ./gradlew pluginZip writes build/distributions/dev.example.hello-1.0.0.zip. In the Jasper you use every day, choose File › Manage Plugins…, then Install from Zip… in the page's Plugin options menu (the three-dot button beside the search field), and pick the zip. The Install Hello sheet shows the name, version, vendor and capabilities ("It asks for no access to your terminals."); Install stages it, and it loads after Restart Now. See Distribution.

    To build against jars you made from a checkout, pass their folder: ./gradlew -PjasperSdkDir=/path/to/jasper/build/sdk-release check pluginZip. -PjasperSdkVersion=<v> picks the jars of another release.

    Next steps

    • Contributions lists every way a plugin adds to the workstation, with the entry API.
    • Lifecycle and Threading are the rules every plugin follows.
    • UI builds tool windows, dialogs and pages from declarative views.
    • Capabilities lists what a terminal, palette or session plugin must declare.

    Manifest

    Every plugin describes itself in plugin.toml, a TOML file at the root of exactly one of its jars (in a Gradle build, src/main/resources/plugin.toml). Jasper reads it at launch, before it loads any of the plugin's classes, and when a user installs the plugin's zip. The file may be at most 64 KiB.

    id = "dev.example.tool"
name = "Example Tool"
version = "1.2.0"
entry = "dev.example.tool.ToolPlugin"
sdk = ">=0.21.0, <0.22"
description = "Runs the team's deploy checks from the command palette."
vendor = "Example"
homepage = "https://example.dev/tool"
icon = "dev/example/tool/tool.svg"
icon_hue = "green"
icon_selected_ink = "foreground"
capabilities = ["palette.contribute", "terminal.inject"]
exports = ["dev.example.tool.api"]
requires = [{ id = "dev.jasper.vault", version = ">=0.2", optional = true }]

[[subcommands]]
name = "deploy-check"
summary = "Run the deploy checks for the current folder"

    Keys

    Only the keys below are allowed; any other top-level key makes the manifest invalid ("Unknown key: key").

    KeyTypeRequiredRules
    idstringyesMatches [a-z][a-z0-9_.-]{0,127}; jasper and ids starting jasper. are reserved. It namespaces what the plugin adds: action, menu, panel, window, status item, palette scope, notification group and file source ids start with <id>., as do the topics it publishes, and icon names start with <id>:. Icon names allow no _, so a plugin that registers icons keeps its id to letters, digits, dots and dashes.
    namestringyesShown everywhere Jasper names the plugin. It must show something: not only spaces, zero-width or bidi characters.
    versionstringyesOne to three numeric components, such as 1, 1.2 or 1.2.0, without leading zeros, pre-release or build suffixes. Missing components are 0, and PluginInfo.version() reads the normalised form, 1.2.0.
    entrystringyesThe fully qualified name of the entry class, in a package. It must be public, have a public no-argument constructor and implement Plugin.
    sdkstringyesThe SDK versions the plugin runs on, as a range (see Versions). A plugin whose range excludes this Jasper's SDK does not load.
    descriptionstringnoShown on the plugin's Overview tab in Settings › Plugins and matched by its search.
    vendorstringnoShown in the plugin list, its details and the review and install sheets ("From vendor").
    capabilitiesarray of stringsnoEach one of the twelve names in Capabilities; an unknown name makes the manifest invalid. A user-installed plugin loads only after the user allows all of them.
    exportsarray of stringsnoPackage names ([a-z_][a-z0-9_]*(\.[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*)*) other plugins may use. Each names exactly one package; a subpackage is exported only when it is listed too. dev.jasper.sdk, dev.jasper.app, dev.jasper.terminal, dev.jasper.buddy, java, javax, jdk and their subpackages are reserved. See Services.
    requiresarray of tablesnoOther plugins this one uses; see below.
    iconstringnoThe path of an .svg or .png file in the plugin's jars, at most 256 KiB. Another extension is logged and ignored; a missing, empty or larger file shows the generic plugin icon. See plugin icons.
    homepagestringnoAn absolute http or https address, shown as "Plugin homepage ↗" on the Details tab. Anything else is logged and ignored.
    icon_huestringnoThe tile behind the icon: neutral (the default), blue, green, amber or purple. A palette scope that names no hue takes it too. Another value is logged and neutral is used.
    icon_selected_inkstringnoauthored (the default) keeps the icon's own colours on a selected row; foreground draws it in the selected row's text colour. Another value is logged and authored is used.
    subcommandsarray of tablesnoThe jasper subcommands the plugin answers; see below.
    presentationstringnoThe jar path of the plugin's kit file, which makes the plugin a look. It needs the presentation.provide capability, and that capability needs this key. See looks.
    themesarray of stringsnoJar paths of theme files, each named <theme id>.json with an id of lowercase letters, digits and dashes; no id twice. See creating themes.
    enabled_by_defaultbooleannotrue unless set. false keeps a plugin bundled in the application off until the user turns it on, as the Enterprise look is; an installed or --plugin-dir plugin ignores it.

    Jar paths in presentation and themes are /-separated segments of lowercase letters, digits, _, . and -, without . or .. segments or a leading /.

    requires

    Each entry names another plugin. Write them as an inline array or as [[requires]] tables:

    [[requires]]
id = "dev.example.core"
version = ">=2.1"

[[requires]]
id = "dev.jasper.snippets"
version = ">=0.1"
optional = true
    KeyMeaning
    idRequired. A valid plugin id other than the plugin's own; no id twice.
    versionA range the other plugin's version must be in. Absent or empty admits any version.
    optionalA boolean, false unless set.

    A hard requirement (optional absent or false) must be met for the plugin to load: when the other plugin is missing or outside the range, this one is skipped ("requires id, which is not available" or "requires id range; found version"), and when the other one fails to start or is skipped, so is this one ("requires id, which failed to start"). An optional requirement never keeps the plugin from loading, and its version range is not checked. Either kind makes the other plugin start first and, when it loads, gives this plugin the packages it exports and the services it publishes; either kind counts toward a dependency cycle, which skips every plugin in it.

    subcommands

    Each [[subcommands]] table declares one jasper <name> command, which the plugin answers with CommandLine.handle(String, CommandHandler):

    KeyRules
    nameRequired. Matches [a-z][a-z0-9-]*; help and version are reserved; no name twice.
    summaryRequired. One visible line without tabs, shown by jasper --help.

    When two plugins declare the same name, a plugin that loads wins over one that does not, then a bundled plugin, then the lowest plugin id; a loading plugin that loses gets the notification "A plugin command was not added". See subcommands.

    Errors

    A manifest that is not valid TOML, lacks a required key, has a key of the wrong type or breaks a rule above is invalid, and the plugin does not load: Jasper posts "A plugin could not be read" in the Plugin problems notification group with the reason after the plugin's folder, for example "Missing required key: entry" or "capabilities names an unknown capability: terminal.read". The same happens when no jar or more than one jar holds a plugin.toml, when it is larger than 64 KiB, and when a folder in Jasper home's plugins is not named after the plugin's id. A zip with such a manifest is refused when the user installs it. The values Jasper only logs and ignores (icon, homepage, icon_hue, icon_selected_ink) never keep a plugin from loading.

    Other files in the jar

    A settings.toml at the root of one of the plugin's jars, at most 1 MiB, is the plugin's settings file as it starts out: the first launch that finds the plugin copies it to plugins/<id>/<id>.toml in Jasper home; a later launch never replaces that file. Write it as commented examples of your settings. Without one, the file starts with a one-line header. See Settings.

    Lifecycle

    Jasper loads plugins once per launch, before its first window opens, and stops them when it quits. A plugin's life is two calls on its entry class, Plugin.start(PluginContext) and Plugin.stop(), both on the UI thread, with one PluginContext that attributes everything the plugin does to it.

    At launch

    1. Discover. Jasper looks in the application's bundled plugins, in plugins/<id>/jars/ in Jasper home, and in the --plugin-dir folder (its jars/ folder, or the jars directly in it). In Jasper home a plugin's folder must be named after its id. Exactly one of a plugin's jars holds its manifest.
    2. Pick one copy of each id. The higher version wins; on equal versions the --plugin-dir copy beats an installed one, which beats the bundled one. The copy that loses is ignored.
    3. Admit. The plugin's sdk range must include this Jasper's SDK, the user must not have disabled it, and an installed plugin must have the user's consent to every capability it declares. In safe mode no installed plugin and no look loads.
    4. Resolve. Plugins in a dependency cycle are skipped, then every plugin whose hard requirement is not loading, and at most one look is chosen.
    5. Load. Each plugin gets its own class loader, dependencies first. Loading refuses a jar with a class in a reserved package (dev.jasper.sdk, dev.jasper.app, dev.jasper.terminal, dev.jasper.buddy, java, javax, jdk) or in a package a dependency exports, a class file larger than 16 MiB, and a class that refers to an SDK type or member this SDK no longer has ("rebuild it for SDK version"). The entry class must be public, have a public no-argument constructor and implement Plugin.
    6. Start. Jasper calls each plugin's start on the UI thread, in load order.

    Load order puts every plugin a plugin requires, hard or optional, before it; otherwise plugins go in alphabetical order of id. A plugin whose hard requirement did not become active is skipped with the reason ("requires id, which failed to start", "was skipped" or "is not running"). What became of each plugin is logged as one line per plugin, shown in Settings › Plugins, and, for a plugin that could not be read, loaded or started, posted in the Plugin problems notification group; see plugins.

    start

    start registers the plugin's contributions and returns. It runs on the UI thread, which draws every window, so it must return promptly: Jasper logs any plugin callback on the UI thread that takes more than 100 ms ("Slow plugin callback on the UI thread"). Move slow work, such as reading files or connecting, to PluginContext.background(). Two things are possible only while start runs: declaring settings with PluginSettings.declare(SettingSpec) (and giving a settings page with PluginSettings.page(SettingsPanel)), and publishing services with Services.publish(Class, Object) or Services.publishPerConsumer(Class, Function). start is also where to look up the services of the plugins it requires: Jasper prepares them before it calls start, and Services.find(Class) returns them.

    public final class ToolPlugin implements Plugin {
    @Override public void start(PluginContext context) {
        Setting<Boolean> enabled = context.settings().declare(SettingSpec.of("enabled", SettingKind.bool(), true)
            .label("Show the deploy action").applies(Applies.RESTART));
        context.log().log(System.Logger.Level.INFO, "Tool " + context.plugin().version() + " started");
        if (!enabled.get()) return;
        context.actions().register(ActionSpec.of("dev.example.tool.deploy", "Run Deploy Checks"),
            invoked -> context.background().execute(() -> runChecks(context)));
    }

    private static void runChecks(PluginContext context) {
        // Slow work runs here, off the UI thread.
    }
}

    When start fails

    When start throws, or the entry class cannot be created, Jasper rolls the plugin back completely: everything the context handed out goes, not only its registrations. Its actions, menus, toolbar and status items, tool windows, windows and dialogs, palette scopes, file sources, subcommand handlers and event subscriptions are removed; open activities end as failed with "Plugin failed to start" and connections close; its notifications expire; staged services are discarded, so no other plugin ever sees them; its background tasks are interrupted; and the context closes. The plugin is reported as failed with "Name failed to start" (with Disable Plugin and Show more…, which opens the Errors window at its stack trace), and plugins that require it are skipped. stop is never called after a failed start.

    stop

    stop is called once, when Jasper quits, for each plugin that started, in reverse start order. It runs before Jasper closes what the plugin left open, so it can save state or end connections cleanly; afterwards Jasper removes every registration as it does after a failed start, and activities still open end as failed with "Plugin stopped". It must not block: Jasper cannot abandon a blocked UI thread, and a stop that does not return ends the process at the exit deadline. See Threading for the shutdown order.

    The context

    Each plugin gets its own PluginContext. Its members are the SDK's entry points:

    MemberWhat it gives
    PluginContext.plugin()The plugin's PluginInfo: id, name, normalised version and the capabilities it holds.
    PluginContext.log()Its logger.
    PluginContext.dataDirectory()Its private data folder.
    PluginContext.background()Its executor for slow work.
    PluginContext.settings()Declared settings and the Settings page.
    PluginContext.events()The event bus: Jasper's topics, other plugins' topics and its own.
    PluginContext.services()Services it publishes and those of the plugins it requires.
    PluginContext.activities()Activities and connections shown on Desk Buddy.
    PluginContext.notifications()Its notification groups.
    PluginContext.actions(), PluginContext.menus(), PluginContext.toolbar(), PluginContext.statusBar(), PluginContext.rail()Commands and where they appear; see Contributions.
    PluginContext.panels(), PluginContext.windows()Tool windows, windows, dialogs, overlays, popovers, content tabs and file choosers.
    PluginContext.kit(), PluginContext.appearance()Its view kit, the current theme's colours, the look Jasper runs with and the saved terminal font.
    PluginContext.terminals()Windows, tabs and panes; see Terminals.
    PluginContext.palette()Command palette scopes; see Palette.
    PluginContext.fileSources()Places in Jasper's file chooser.
    PluginContext.commandLine()Its jasper subcommands.
    PluginContext.platform()Desktop integration: the editor, the browser and the clipboard.

    After a failed start, and after stop, the context is closed: calls that contribute throw IllegalStateException, PluginContext.background() rejects tasks with RejectedExecutionException, and the handles it issued stop working. Queries and commands on window, tab and pane handles throw IllegalStateException ("Plugin context is closed: id"), and so do the kit's view methods ("Plugin kit is closed"); sending text, bytes or a paste to a pane does nothing; and Setting.set(Object) fails with "The plugin has stopped." PluginContext.log() keeps working, so a background task that outlives the plugin can still say why it ended.

    Logging

    PluginContext.log() is a System.Logger named dev.jasper.plugins.<id>. Its records go to Jasper's log, jasper-<u>-<g>.log in the logs folder of Jasper home, beside Jasper's own; records at INFO and above are written. Every failure Jasper contains in the plugin's code is logged there at WARNING as "Plugin id failed in what" with its stack trace. See diagnostics.

    Data and settings

    PluginContext.dataDirectory() is plugins/<id>/data/ in Jasper home, created when missing. The plugin owns its contents. It survives updates and disabling, and is deleted, with the plugin's jars and settings file, when the user removes an installed plugin. The settings file beside it, plugins/<id>/<id>.toml, belongs to declared settings; read and write it through them rather than as a file.

    Safe mode and --plugin-dir

    jasper --safe-mode starts Jasper without any plugin installed in Jasper home and without any look; bundled plugins that provide no look, and a --plugin-dir plugin, still load. jasper --plugin-dir <folder> loads the plugin in that folder beside the others, without a capability review, as a separate, standalone Jasper that never hands off to the one already running. Use it to run the plugin you are building; see the command line. A Jasper started with --plugin-dir, --safe-mode, --config or --standalone answers the jasper command only in its own shells and does not update the subcommand list jasper --help prints: try a plugin's subcommand from a shell inside the --plugin-dir Jasper.

    Threading

    Jasper's UI thread is the Swing event dispatch thread. It draws every window and runs every plugin's start, stop, handlers and callbacks, one at a time. That gives plugins a simple model: code that Jasper calls runs on the UI thread unless its documentation says otherwise, never at the same time as other UI-thread code, and must return promptly. Slow work goes to the plugin's background executor, and results come back to the UI thread before they touch the SDK.

    The UI thread rule

    Registering anything (actions, menus, toolbar and status items, tool windows, windows, palette scopes, file sources, subcommands, event subscriptions, services), creating and updating views, and every query or command on Terminals and its handles must happen on the UI thread. A call from another thread throws IllegalStateException: "what must be called on the UI thread: plugin id", or "Kit requires EDT" from the view kit. The exceptions are listed per type in the API reference; the main ones:

    Safe from any threadNote
    Events.publish(Topic, Object)Publication only enqueues; handlers run later on the UI thread.
    Subscription.close()Idempotent and never throws. On the UI thread the contribution is gone when it returns; from another thread at most one delivery already under way may still complete.
    Activities.begin(ActivitySpec), ActivityHandle, ConnectionHandleReport progress and state from the thread doing the work.
    NotificationGroup.post(NotificationSpec) and its shortcuts, NotificationHandlePosting returns at once.
    Setting.get(), Setting.set(Object)A successful save completes its future on the UI thread; a failed one may complete it on another thread, so hop to the UI thread before touching the UI.
    Services.find(Class), Services.require(Class)Cache reads that run no provider code.
    PaneHandle.sendText(String), PaneHandle.sendBytes(byte[]), PaneHandle.paste(String)Calls from one thread keep their order.
    PendingSessionEvery method, also after the plugin stopped.
    CommandCall.out(String), CommandCall.err(String)Write to the caller's terminal while the call runs.
    Platform.openInEditor(Path), Platform.browse(URI)They do their work in the background.
    Appearance.variant(), Appearance.workspaceVariant()Whether the chrome or the workspace is dark or light.
    Appearance.presentation()The look Jasper runs with, the same value until it restarts.
    Appearance.terminalTypography()The saved terminal font; it already returns a new value when its change handlers run.

    A few callbacks run off the UI thread, and must not touch Swing or UI-thread-only SDK methods:

    • FileBrowser's methods run on one of Jasper's worker threads, one call at a time, and may block.
    • TerminalConnection: output is read on the session's reader thread, input and resize are used on its writer thread, and close runs on Jasper's cleanup thread.
    • PendingSession.onCancelled(Runnable) handlers run on the cleanup thread.
    • The future PaneHandle.foregroundJob() returns completes on a worker thread.

    Containment

    Every call Jasper makes into plugin code is contained: an Exception or LinkageError is caught, logged against the plugin, counted on its Details tab in Settings › Plugins and recorded as an incident, and Jasper carries on. The failure is posted in the Plugin problems group as "Name failed in what" with Disable Plugin and Show more…. A failing callback fails only itself: a throwing event handler does not affect other subscribers, a throwing palette search shows no rows, a throwing panel factory shows "This panel could not be loaded." A UI-thread callback that takes more than 100 ms is logged at INFO with its duration.

    Background work

    PluginContext.background() is the plugin's executor. In Jasper each task runs on a virtual thread of its own (named jasper-plugin-<id>-<n>), so tasks may run at the same time; a task that throws is contained like any other callback. To come back to the UI thread, post to the event dispatch thread, as the bundled plugins do:

    context.actions().register(ActionSpec.of("dev.example.tool.count", "Count Log Lines"), invoked ->
    context.background().execute(() -> {
        long lines;
        try (var stream = Files.lines(context.dataDirectory().resolve("events.log"))) { lines = stream.count(); }
        catch (IOException failure) {
            context.notifications().group().error("Could not count the lines", failure);
            return;
        }
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> context.notifications().group().info("Log lines", lines + " lines"));
    }));

    Posting a notification is safe from any thread, so this example would work without invokeLater; anything that needs the UI thread, such as updating a view or a status item, does need it.

    Subscriptions and lifetimes

    Most registrations return a Subscription, or a handle that is one: PluginAction, PluginMenu, StatusItem, StatusProgress, UiView, UiAnchor, PluginPopover and every dialog (WindowSurface). Closing it ends that one registration. Declared settings, a settings page, published services and notification groups are not; they last until the plugin stops. A ContentTab closes, without asking, with ContentTab.close() or when the plugin stops. A plugin rarely needs to close anything: when it stops, Jasper closes whatever it left open, newest first. Close a subscription when the contribution should go away while the plugin keeps running, such as a menu entry for a host the user deleted, or rebuild a menu section with PluginMenu.clear() and PluginMenu.add(String).

    Some handles end on their own: a PanelHost when its window closes (PanelHost.onClosed(Runnable)), a ContentTab when the user closes it (ContentTab.onClosed(Runnable)), a UiAnchor when its control is hidden, disabled, made busy, removed or closed (UiAnchor.onClosed(Runnable)), and a dialog when the user or its window closes it (WindowSurface.onClosed(Runnable)). Pane, tab and window handles keep only an id: a closed target is simply absent, queries return the last known value, and commands to it are ignored.

    Window owners

    A WindowOwner is something a dialog, chooser or tab belongs to. Three handles are owners: a Jasper window (WindowHandle), one of the plugin's content tabs (ContentTab) and an anchor on a mounted control (UiAnchor). The owner decides where the surface appears and how long it lives:

    • DialogSpec's owner must be open when the dialog is created. A dialog owned by an anchor closes when the anchor closes; one owned by a content tab closes with the tab, and while a modal one is open the tab can neither close nor move to another window.
    • An overlay (Windows.overlay(OverlaySpec)) closes with its Jasper window.
    • A file chooser (Windows.choose(FileChoice) and the choose* methods) is cancelled, and its result discarded, when its owner closes or the plugin stops.
    • Windows.openTab(ContentSpec, WindowOwner, UiView) opens the tab in the owner's window, or the main window.

    Shutdown

    Before Jasper quits or restarts it asks the closing guards: the content tabs' Windows.onTabsClosing(BiFunction) guards, then the Windows.onQuitting(Supplier) guards, one at a time. One that refuses cancels the quit, and nothing has closed yet. Then, on the UI thread, for each plugin that started, in reverse start order:

    1. Jasper calls its Plugin.stop().
    2. Jasper closes everything the plugin left open: registrations, dialogs, content tabs, views, provided sessions still connecting, notifications, activities ("Plugin stopped") and connections. A secret it copied with Platform.copySecret(String) is cleared from the clipboard if it is still there, and a subcommand call still running ends with exit code 1.
    3. The plugin's background executor stops accepting tasks. Tasks already running get 1.5 seconds to finish, then are interrupted.

    The whole shutdown is bounded: a stop or handler that blocks the UI thread ends the process at the exit deadline, and the log names the plugin callback that was running. A connection a session plugin attached belongs to its pane, which Jasper closes with its window.

    On macOS a resident Jasper answers Cmd+Q, Jasper › Quit, the Dock's Quit and a Jasper window's File › Quit by closing its windows and staying in the background. That asks the tabs' closing guards but not the quit guards, and the plugins keep running until Jasper really quits.

    Capabilities

    A capability names something a plugin does that the user cannot see in the window, such as reading what a terminal runs or typing into it, or a role only one plugin at a time can take. Adding actions, menu items, tool windows, windows, status items, notifications, settings and services needs none. A plugin declares its capabilities in plugin.toml:

    capabilities = ["terminal.observe", "terminal.inject", "palette.contribute"]

    The names are the constants of Capabilities; Capabilities.ALL lists them. An unknown name makes the manifest invalid.

    CapabilityConstantWhat it allowsSince
    terminal.observeTERMINAL_OBSERVEPane metadata, working directories, titles, command text, and every jasper.terminal.* topic.
    terminal.selectionTERMINAL_SELECTIONReading the text selected in a pane.
    terminal.injectTERMINAL_INJECTTyping and pasting into a pane.
    terminal.openTERMINAL_OPENOpening local tabs and splits (the shell, a shell profile or a program), and reading the shell profiles with Terminals.profiles() and onProfilesChanged.
    session.provideSESSION_PROVIDEProviding a pane's session, such as a remote connection.
    palette.contributePALETTE_CONTRIBUTEContribute command-palette scopes and open the palette.
    files.sourceFILES_SOURCEAdd places, such as saved hosts, to Jasper's file chooser.0.10.0
    network.listenNETWORK_LISTENAccepting connections from other programs or computers, such as serving files. Nothing gates it: the user consents to it when the plugin is installed.0.11.0
    clipboard.readCLIPBOARD_READReading the text on the clipboard with Platform.clipboardText(); the clipboard often holds something the user just copied elsewhere, such as a password. Writing needs no capability.0.16.1
    terminal.environmentTERMINAL_ENVIRONMENTAdding variables, such as EDITOR, to the environment of new local shells and of the programs that LocalSpec.command runs in tabs and splits, with Terminals.environment.0.17.1
    editor.provideEDITOR_PROVIDEBeing the editor Jasper opens files with, through Platform.editor.0.17.1
    presentation.providePRESENTATION_PROVIDEProviding Jasper's presentation, the window chrome and controls, from the next start. One plugin at a time provides it, and it needs no call: the host reads the presentation from the plugin's descriptor.0.18.0

    Consent

    A plugin the user installed loads only after the user has allowed every capability it declares. The review sheet in Settings › Plugins lists them in the user's words (in the table below), each followed by its name in brackets, with the warning that a plugin is not sandboxed; Allow and Enable records exactly the capabilities shown. A later version that declares a capability the user has not allowed waits for a new review and does not load until then; one that declares the same or fewer keeps the consent. Bundled plugins and the --plugin-dir plugin need no review.

    So the capabilities a running plugin holds are exactly those it declares: PluginInfo.capabilities() from PluginContext.plugin() lists them, and a plugin that can do without one checks before it calls:

    if (!context.plugin().capabilities().contains(Capabilities.TERMINAL_INJECT)) {
    context.log().log(System.Logger.Level.INFO, "Typing into panes needs terminal.inject");
    return;
}

    What each capability guards

    CapabilityThe review sheet saysCalls that need itAudit log
    terminal.observeSee your terminals: titles, folders, the commands you run and how they endPaneHandle.info(), PaneHandle.foregroundJob(), TabHandle.title(), and subscribing to any TerminalEvents topic (every id starting jasper.terminal.)The first terminal subscription
    terminal.selectionRead the text you select in a terminalPaneHandle.selection()Each read, with the number of characters
    terminal.injectType into your terminalsPaneHandle.sendText(String), PaneHandle.sendBytes(byte[]), PaneHandle.paste(String), also on a palette query's target paneEach call, with the number of bytes
    terminal.openOpen terminal tabs, splits and windows, and run programs in themTerminals.openTab(WindowHandle, OpenRequest) and Terminals.split(PaneHandle, Direction, OpenRequest) with a local request (a shell, a shell profile or a program), Terminals.profiles(), Terminals.onProfilesChanged(Runnable)Each open, with the program's file name when it runs one
    session.provideRun its own terminal sessions, such as remote connectionsopenTab and split with OpenRequest.session(SessionSpec)Each open
    palette.contributeAdd scopes to the command palette and open itPalette.register(PaletteScope) and Palette.open(WindowHandle, String, Optional, Optional)The first use
    files.sourceAdd places, such as saved hosts, to the file chooserFileSources.register(FileSource)The first registration
    network.listenAccept connections from other programs or computers, such as serving filesNo call. It tells the user, before they allow the plugin, that it accepts connections.
    clipboard.readRead text you copied to the clipboardPlatform.clipboardText(); writing to the clipboard needs nothingEach read, with the number of characters
    terminal.environmentSet environment variables in new terminal shellsTerminals.environment(Function)The registration
    editor.provideOpen the files Jasper opens for editingPlatform.editor(FileEditor)The registration
    presentation.provideChange Jasper's window chrome and controls after a restartNo call. It goes with the manifest's presentation key, each requiring the other; see looks.

    Finding windows, tabs and panes, focusing and selecting them, and reading an action's window and pane need no capability; what a handle may then do does.

    MissingCapabilityException

    A gated call by a plugin that does not hold the capability throws MissingCapabilityException with the message "Plugin id needs the capability capability; declare it in plugin.toml"; MissingCapabilityException.pluginId() and MissingCapabilityException.capability() name both. Pane, tab and terminal calls check the capability before anything else, so a missing declaration shows even on a closed pane or from the wrong thread. Thrown inside a callback, it is contained and reported like any other failure.

    The audit log

    Jasper logs the gated calls marked above on the logger dev.jasper.app.plugins.audit, at INFO, as "Plugin id used capability: what", for example "Plugin dev.example.tool used terminal.inject: typed 12 bytes into pane …". It records amounts and targets, never content.

    Capabilities cover the calls a plugin makes to Jasper. They do not limit what the plugin's own code does with the Java runtime: it can read and write the user's files, open connections and start programs like any program the user runs. The class loader that hides Jasper's internals keeps plugins on the public API; it is not a security boundary either. Declare only what you use: the list is what the user is asked to allow.

    Contributions

    Everything a plugin adds to the workstation goes through its PluginContext. Jasper draws all of it in its own style and the current look, so a contribution looks built in, and removes all of it when the plugin stops. Ids are namespaced: they start with the plugin's id and a dot. Registration needs the UI thread and an open context.

    Map

    ContributionEntry pointCapabilityWhere it appears
    ActionsActions.register(ActionSpec, Consumer)The command palette of every window, Settings › Keymap and its default shortcut; then wherever the plugin places it
    Menu entriesMenus.standard(StandardMenu), Menus.create(String, String), Menus.terminalContext()A section at the end of a built-in menu, a top-level menu of its own, the pane right-click menu
    Toolbar itemsToolbar.add(ToolbarItem)In the main window's toolbar, after Jasper's Split and Maximize buttons and before Find and Settings
    Status items and progressStatusBar.add(StatusItemSpec), StatusBar.addProgress(StatusItemSpec)Either end of the main window's status bar
    Rail buttonsRail.add(String)The left tool window stripe, after the tool window buttons
    Tool windowsPanels.register(PanelSpec, PanelFactory), Panels.toggle(String, WindowHandle)A stripe button and a tool window in one of six dock slots of the main window; View › Tool Windows
    DialogsWindows.dialog(DialogSpec), Windows.overlay(OverlaySpec), Windows.popover(UiAnchor)Dialogs and sheets, in-window overlays, popovers below a control
    Content tabsWindows.openTab(ContentSpec, WindowOwner, UiView, TabPlacement)A document in a pane of a workspace tab, beside terminals, a new pane or a new child window
    Split itemsWindows.splitItem(SplitItemSpec, BiConsumer)Every Split list, after the terminal, with two bindable actions
    RestorersWindows.restorer(String, TabRestorer)The plugin's saved tabs coming back when Jasper restores its windows
    File choosersWindows.choose(FileChoice), Windows.chooseFiles(WindowOwner, String, Optional), Windows.chooseDirectory(WindowOwner, String, Optional), Windows.chooseSaveFile(WindowOwner, String, Optional)Jasper's file chooser, over a Jasper window or one of the plugin's content tabs
    Places in the file chooserFileSources.register(FileSource)files.sourceA section in the chooser's navigation pane, such as Remote's saved hosts
    Palette scopesPalette.register(PaletteScope)palette.contributeThe command palette and the Run window; see Palette
    NotificationsNotifications.group(), Notifications.group(GroupSpec)Cards, history and Settings › Appearance & Behavior › Notifications
    Activities and connectionsActivities.begin(ActivitySpec), Activities.connection(ConnectionSpec)Desk Buddy's cards, and outcome notifications
    Local tabs, splits and programsTerminals.openTab(WindowHandle, OpenRequest), Terminals.split(PaneHandle, Direction, OpenRequest) with a local requestterminal.openTerminal tabs and panes; see Terminals
    Provided sessionsThe same calls with OpenRequest.session(SessionSpec)session.provideA pane whose session the plugin connects, such as SSH
    Shell environmentTerminals.environment(Function)terminal.environmentVariables in new local shells (not WSL profiles) and programs
    Subcommands[[subcommands]] in the manifest and CommandLine.handle(String, CommandHandler)jasper <name> in a shell
    The editor rolePlatform.editor(FileEditor)editor.provideThe files Jasper opens for editing, and Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Linux and Windows) on paths in terminals
    SettingsPluginSettings.declare(SettingSpec), PluginSettings.page(SettingsPanel)The plugin's page in Settings › Tools; see Settings
    IconsUiKit.registerIcon(IconAsset)Anywhere the plugin names an icon
    Services and topicsServices.publish(Class, Object), Events.publish(Topic, Object)Other plugins; see Services
    Quit and close guardsWindows.onQuitting(Supplier), Windows.onTabsClosing(BiFunction), WindowSurface.onClosing(BooleanSupplier)Asked before Jasper quits or a window or tab closes
    A look and themespresentation and themes in the manifestpresentation.provide for a lookThe chrome and controls, and themes in Settings › Appearance & Behavior › Appearance; see looks and creating themes

    Actions and shortcuts

    An action is a command: an id, a title, an optional icon and keywords, and a handler that runs on the UI thread with an ActionContext, which names the window it was invoked in and the pane it concerns (the pane under a context menu, otherwise the window's focused pane). Registering an action lists it in every window's command palette and in Settings › Keymap under the plugin's name; then place it:

    String run = "dev.example.tool.run";
PluginAction action = context.actions().register(ActionSpec.of(run, "Run Deploy Checks")
        .withIcon("play").withKeywords(List.of("deploy", "check")).withDefaultBinding("cmd+alt+d"),
    invoked -> invoked.pane().ifPresent(pane ->
        context.log().log(System.Logger.Level.INFO, "Checks requested for pane " + pane.id())));
context.menus().standard(StandardMenu.TOOLS).add(run);
context.menus().terminalContext().add(run);
context.toolbar().add(ToolbarItem.action(run));
context.rail().add(run);

    PluginAction.setEnabled(boolean) and PluginAction.setTitle(String) change it everywhere it appears; closing it removes it and every placement. Placements may name only the plugin's own actions.

    A default shortcut is written in the configuration syntax (cmd, ctrl, alt, shift and a key, such as cmd+alt+d). On macOS it applies as written. On Linux and Windows cmd means Ctrl+Shift, and a default that names cmd and shift also gets Alt: cmd+alt+d is Cmd+Option+D on macOS and Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D on Linux and Windows. ActionSpec.withDefaultBindings(String, String) gives a separate Linux and Windows default instead, naming ctrl, alt and shift literally, or null for none there. The user's [keybindings] entry for the action's id wins over the default; a default that collides with a shortcut already in use is dropped, and Jasper's log records "Default shortcut '…' is already used by '…'; bind the action under [keybindings] to give it one." See keyboard shortcuts.

    ActionSpec.withContext(ShortcutContext) limits where the shortcut applies:

    ContextApplies
    ShortcutContext.global()Anywhere in a Jasper window; the default.
    ShortcutContext.terminal()In a terminal pane, including its find bar.
    ShortcutContext.content()In a content tab the plugin opened.
    ShortcutContext.panel(String)Inside one of the plugin's tool windows.

    Where focus is, the most specific applicable action runs: a panel or content action, then a terminal one, then a global one. A key whose action does not apply there reaches the focused component, such as the shell. So does a disabled action's key, except in a terminal pane, where it does nothing.

    Menus

    Menus.standard(StandardMenu) returns a new section at the end of File, Edit, View, Tab, Tools, Session or Transfer, after a separator. Jasper has no Tools, Session or Transfer items of its own, so those menus show only while a plugin has entries in them: Tools for utility commands, Session for connecting to hosts and working with sessions, Transfer for file browsers, transfers and file servers. Menus.create(String, String) adds a top-level menu, placed with the other plugins' menus. Menus.terminalContext() is a section at the end of every pane's right-click menu; an action run from it receives that pane. A section is a PluginMenu: add actions, separators and submenus, and rebuild it at any time with PluginMenu.clear().

    Toolbar

    ToolbarItem.action(String) is a button for one action, ToolbarItem.menu(String, String, List) a button that opens a menu of actions, and ToolbarItem.view(ToolbarViewFactory) a small group of the plugin's own controls in the main window's toolbar (a child window has none). A toolbar view's root is an INLINE Nodes.Stack of LABEL texts, DROPDOWN, SEARCHABLE or PICKER choices, at most one PRIMARY button, icon-only GHOST buttons (a blank label with an icon and a tooltip, which need SDK 0.18.1 or later), menu buttons and separators; any other tree is refused, and the window shows no view. When the toolbar is too narrow, buttons move into its "More actions" menu and a view hides.

    Status bar

    StatusItem status = context.statusBar().add(new StatusItemSpec("dev.example.tool.status", Side.RIGHT, 100));
status.setText("Deploys: 3");
status.setTooltip("Run the deploy checks");
status.setAction("dev.example.tool.run");

    One handle drives the item in the main window's status bar; a child window has none. Side.LEFT items follow the shell and folder, Side.RIGHT items precede the terminal size and configuration state, and items on a side are ordered by ascending priority. An item with an action is a button; without one it is plain text. StatusBar.addProgress(StatusItemSpec) adds a progress control that StatusProgress.update(StatusProgressState) drives, with a fraction or none and up to two actions.

    Tool windows and the rail

    A registered panel gets a stripe button in the main window, the only window with tool windows: its icon, or under the Enterprise look's labelled stripes a label that starts with the icon and reads its title. Its PanelFactory builds its view once, on the UI thread, the first time the panel shows; a toggle from a child window shows it in the main window and brings that window to the front. The PanelSpec's anchor and PanelSpec.withSplit() pick the default slot (Left Top, Left Bottom, Bottom Left, Right Top, Right Bottom or Bottom Right); the user can move it with the header's Options menu, and Jasper remembers where. Unless the spec names a toggle action of the plugin's own (PanelSpec.withToggleActionId(String)), Jasper registers <panel id>.toggle, titled "Toggle title", with no default shortcut, and View › Tool Windows lists it. PanelHost is the panel's place in the main window: PanelHost.show(), PanelHost.hide(), PanelHost.setHeader(PanelHeader) for a detail, a status dot and icon actions in the header. A factory that throws shows "This panel could not be loaded." Under the Enterprise look, whose tool windows are flush, the toggle action makes the tool window it shows the active one, which takes the keyboard, and activates a showing tool window that is not the active one instead of hiding it; a plugin's own toggle action does this when its handler calls Panels.toggle(String, WindowHandle) or PanelHost.show() for its panel, and any other call only shows or hides. Rail.add(String) adds a plain button for an action, for example one that opens a plugin's tab.

    Dialogs, overlays and popovers

    Jasper builds the frame, title bar, icon and theme of every surface; the plugin fills it with a view through WindowSurface.setContent(UiView) and shows it with WindowSurface.show(). A view of the plugin's own that is not a tool window is a content tab.

    • Windows.dialog(DialogSpec): a dialog over a Jasper window, a content tab or an anchor, closed with its window, presented DialogSpec.Presentation.CENTERED, as an DialogSpec.Presentation.ATTACHED_SHEET or as an in-window DialogSpec.Presentation.OVERLAY; the look may place it another way. show returns after a modal dialog closes.
    • Windows.overlay(OverlaySpec): progress content centred inside a Jasper window, one per window. Escape and outside clicks do not dismiss it, so give it a Cancel action.
    • Windows.popover(UiAnchor): a popup below (or above) a button or picker, from UiView.anchor(String); Escape and clicks outside close it.

    Content tabs

    Windows.openTab(ContentSpec, WindowOwner, UiView) opens a view as a document in a new tab of the owner's window, or of the main window, as the Editor does; Windows.openTab(ContentSpec, WindowOwner, UiView, TabPlacement) opens it where a TabPlacement says: a new tab, a new pane beside the focused one, or a new child window. The ContentSpec's key identifies the document: opening a key the plugin already has open selects that tab and returns its handle. Through the ContentTab the plugin sets the tab's title, detail, icon, unsaved marker and location (ContentTab.setPresentation(ContentPresentation)), its commands (ContentTab.setCommands(List)), which its context menu lists and whose shortcuts apply while it is active, and its status bar items (ContentTab.setStatus(List)). Commands with the ids find, find-next, find-previous, copy and paste answer Jasper's own Find, Find Next, Find Previous, Copy and Paste. The user can move the tab to a new window and back, as ContentTab.moveToNewWindow() and ContentTab.moveToMainWindow() do, and give its pane a tab of its own (ContentTab.moveToNewTab()). Windows.onTabsClosing(BiFunction) decides whether tabs with unsaved work may close.

    Windows.splitItem(SplitItemSpec, BiConsumer) puts a view of the plugin's in every Split list (the Tab menu's and the right-click menus' Split submenus), after the terminal, with two actions, "Split Right with" and "Split Down with" its label; the opener receives the window and the placement. Windows.splitChoices() lists the choices for a menu the plugin builds itself, and ContentTab.split(SplitChoice, Direction) runs one beside the item.

    A tab comes back when Jasper restores its windows if its ContentSpec carries a RestoreState (ContentSpec.withRestore(RestoreState), later ContentTab.setRestore(Optional)) and the plugin registered a TabRestorer for its kind with Windows.restorer(String, TabRestorer). The restorer gets a RestoreRequest on the UI thread, opens the tab as the plugin always does without blocking or asking the user anything, and returns empty, or why the tab cannot come back, which its placeholder then says.

    File choosers and places

    Windows.chooseFiles(WindowOwner, String, Optional), Windows.chooseDirectory(WindowOwner, String, Optional) and Windows.chooseSaveFile(WindowOwner, String, Optional) show Jasper's file chooser for local paths and return absolute, normalised paths, or nothing when the user cancels; saving over an existing file asks first. Windows.choose(FileChoice) also offers the roots of the file sources the FileChoice names and returns FileLocation.Local and FileLocation.Sourced values. A FileChoice opens one or several files, saves to one file with a suggested name, or picks a folder; without an initial location the chooser starts where the owner's focused pane is (in a named source's root when that source locates the pane, otherwise in its local folder), else in the home folder. The owner is an open Jasper window or one of the plugin's content tabs. Call them on the UI thread: they pump UI events until the user answers, so recheck what the result depends on. Closing the owner or stopping the plugin cancels them.

    With files.source, FileSources.register(FileSource) adds places to the chooser, as Remote does with its saved hosts. The source's roots appear under its FileSourceSpec's heading in every chooser whose FileChoice names its id, which starts with the plugin's id and a dot. FileSource.spec() is read once; FileSource.roots() lists the FileRoots (an id, a label, a detail shown as the tooltip, and whether opening it needs no connection or sign-in first); FileSource.onChanged(Runnable) tells the chooser that the roots or their connected state changed; FileSource.locate(PaneHandle) says where a terminal pane is in one of the roots, so a chooser opened from that pane starts there (FileLocation.Sourced.HOME when only the root is known). These run on the UI thread and do no I/O.

    When the user opens a root, Jasper calls FileSource.connect(String, WindowOwner). It may ask the user to sign in over the owner it receives: the Jasper window the chooser belongs to (a content tab's, for a chooser the tab owns), or null when it belongs to none. It returns a stage that completes, on any thread, with a FileBrowser; when the stage is a CompletableFuture, Jasper cancels it to abandon the attempt. Jasper owns the browser and closes it once, when the chooser closes. It calls FileBrowser.home(), FileBrowser.list(String, Consumer), FileBrowser.stat(String), FileBrowser.read(String, int) (the start of a file, for the preview) and FileBrowser.mkdir(String) on the chooser's worker thread, one call at a time and never on the UI thread, so they may block; FileBrowser.abort() interrupts a call from any thread. Paths are absolute and use /. A source method that throws shows no roots, locates nothing or fails to connect ("The plugin could not connect.").

    Notifications

    NotificationGroup deploys = context.notifications().group(
    new GroupSpec("dev.example.tool.deploys", "Deploys", DisplayMode.CARD));
deploys.post(NotificationSpec.of(Severity.WARNING, "Deploy checks failed")
    .withContent("2 of 14 checks failed on staging.")
    .withAction(NotificationAction.of("Show Log",
        () -> context.platform().openInEditor(context.dataDirectory().resolve("deploy.log")))));

    A plugin posts in its default group (Notifications.group(), named after the plugin) or in groups it declares during start, which the user can set to show cards, sticky cards, history only or nothing in Settings › Appearance & Behavior › Notifications. Text is plain: a title of up to 200 characters, content up to 4,000, and up to eight actions. NotificationGroup.error(String, Throwable) attaches the failure, which Jasper records as the plugin's incident and offers with Show more…. Plugins cannot see other notifications. See notifications.

    Activities and connections

    context.background().execute(() -> {
    ActivityHandle activity = context.activities().begin(ActivitySpec.of("Deploy checks"));
    for (int check = 1; check <= 14; check++) activity.progress(check / 14.0, "Check " + check + " of 14");
    activity.succeed("All 14 checks passed");
});

    A running activity shows as a card on Desk Buddy, with its fraction and detail. When it succeeds or fails, Jasper posts the outcome in the plugin's <id>.activities group, so the user can mute outcomes without muting the plugin's other notifications; a cancelled activity posts nothing. ActivitySpec's action, one of the plugin's own, runs when the user clicks the card. A connection (Activities.connection(ConnectionSpec)) has a state instead of an end, up, degraded or down, until the plugin closes it; Desk Buddy shows a card per connection. Both are published on Activities.TOPIC and Activities.CONNECTIONS, which any plugin may follow.

    Subcommands

    A plugin declares each jasper subcommand in its manifest and answers it while it runs:

    [[subcommands]]
name = "deploy-check"
summary = "Run the deploy checks for the current folder"
    context.commandLine().handle("deploy-check", call -> {
    call.out("Checking " + call.workingDirectory() + "\n");
    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(0);
});

    jasper deploy-check … in a shell reaches the running Jasper, which runs the handler on the UI thread with a CommandCall: the arguments after the name, the caller's working directory, the Jasper window the command ran in, and the caller's standard output and error. The stage's value is the exit code (0 to 255; anything else is 1); a handler that throws, or a stage that fails, prints jasper: <name> failed: <message> and exits 1. CommandCall.onCancelled(Runnable) hears Ctrl+C. While no handler is registered, the command prints jasper: <name> is unavailable (the <Name> plugin is off) and exits 1; an unknown name exits 2. A Jasper started with --plugin-dir, --safe-mode, --config or --standalone answers jasper only in its own shells, so try a plugin's subcommand from a shell inside the --plugin-dir Jasper. jasper --help lists the subcommands of the plugins that were running when Jasper last started without those options. CommandLine.client() is the path of the jasper command itself, for a plugin that writes it into another program's settings. See the command line.

    The editor role

    Platform.editor(FileEditor) makes the plugin the editor Jasper opens files with: its configuration files, every Platform.openInEditor(Path) and a Cmd-click (Ctrl-click on Linux and Windows) on a file path in a local terminal pane reach the plugin's FileEditor first; returning false hands the file to the desktop. One plugin at a time holds the role: a bundled plugin's registration replaces one that is not bundled; otherwise the first stays and a later one throws. The Editor plugin takes it. Shell variables (Terminals.environment(Function)) and program tabs (LocalSpec.running(List, Optional)) are described in Terminals.

    Desktop integration

    Platform.copy(String) puts text on the clipboard; Platform.copySecret(String) also clears it 30 seconds later if it is still there. Platform.browse(URI) opens an http or https address in the browser, and Platform.openInEditor(Path) opens a file in the user's editor. Their failures are posted in the plugin's default notification group, never thrown.

    UI

    Plugin UI is declarative. A plugin describes what to show as an immutable tree of Nodes records, a ViewSpec; its UiKit turns the tree into a UiView that Jasper draws. Jasper owns every pixel: colours, fonts, spacing, focus, keyboard behaviour and the current look's control styles, so a plugin's tool window looks and behaves like Jasper's own, in every theme and look. The plugin receives typed UiEvents and answers with UiView.update(ViewSpec). The same views fill tool windows, plugin windows, dialogs, overlays, popovers, content tabs, toolbar groups and settings pages. For worked compositions, see plugin UI.

    A view

    This tool window lists deploy targets and filters them as the user types. The plugin keeps the state (the query and the selection), rebuilds the whole tree from it, and hands the tree to update:

    /** A tool window listing deploy targets, filtered by a search field. */
final class TargetsPanel {
    private final List<String> targets = List.of("staging", "production", "canary");
    private final UiView view;
    private String query = "";
    private Set<String> selected = Set.of();

    TargetsPanel(UiKit kit) { view = kit.create(spec(), this::handle); }

    UiView view() { return view; }

    private void handle(UiEvent event) {
        switch (event) {
            case UiEvent.Edited edited when edited.id().equals("targets.search") -> { query = edited.text(); view.update(spec()); }
            case UiEvent.Selected chosen when chosen.id().equals("targets.rows") -> { selected = chosen.ids(); view.update(spec()); }
            case UiEvent.Action action when action.id().equals("open") -> selected.forEach(this::open);
            default -> { }
        }
    }

    private void open(String target) { /* the row was activated: Enter or a double click */ }

    private ViewSpec spec() {
        var rows = new ArrayList<ListItem>();
        for (String target : targets) {
            if (!target.contains(query.strip())) continue;
            rows.add(new ListItem(target,
                Optional.of(new Nodes.Icon(target + ".icon", ControlState.READY, "server", Nodes.Hue.GREEN, Nodes.IconSize.CONTROL, "Target")),
                List.of(new Nodes.Text(target + ".name", ControlState.READY, target, Nodes.TextRole.BODY)), List.of(), List.of()));
        }
        // A selected id must name a row in this tree.
        var shown = new HashSet<String>();
        rows.forEach(row -> shown.add(row.id()));
        var keep = new HashSet<>(selected);
        keep.retainAll(shown);
        var header = new Nodes.Header("targets.header", ControlState.READY, "Targets", OptionalInt.of(targets.size()),
            Optional.empty(), Optional.empty(), List.of());
        var search = new Nodes.Field("targets.search", ControlState.READY, Nodes.FieldKind.SEARCH, query, "Search targets",
            "Search targets", "");
        var list = new Nodes.ItemList("targets.rows", ControlState.READY, Nodes.ListKind.SINGLE, rows, keep, "open", List.of(),
            Nodes.SelectionMode.SINGLE, Optional.empty());
        return new ViewSpec(new Nodes.Panel("targets", ControlState.READY, header, Optional.of(search), list, Optional.empty()));
    }
}

    Registered as a tool window, in the main window:

    context.panels().register(new PanelSpec("dev.example.tool.targets", "Targets", "server", Anchor.LEFT),
    host -> new TargetsPanel(context.kit()).view());

    Kit and views

    PluginContext.kit() is the plugin's kit. UiKit.create(ViewSpec, Consumer) makes a view the plugin owns, with a handler that receives its events on the UI thread; a handler that throws is contained. Kit and view methods run on the UI thread. A view is mounted in one place: a PanelFactory or ToolbarViewFactory returns it, WindowSurface.setContent(UiView), PluginPopover.setContent(UiView) and Windows.openTab(ContentSpec, WindowOwner, UiView) take it, and SettingsPanel.create(SettingsPanelHost) returns it. Mounting a view already mounted elsewhere, or another plugin's view, is refused. Replacing a surface's content or closing the surface closes its view; closing a view is idempotent, and the plugin's views close when it stops.

    View methodWhat it does
    UiView.update(ViewSpec)Replaces the tree, reconciling by node id and kind. Calling it from inside an update throws.
    UiView.spec()The tree as last given, without the user's pending edits or any secret.
    UiView.focus(String), UiView.reveal(String)Focus a node; scroll one into view without moving focus.
    UiView.selectAll(String)Select a field's text without editing it or moving focus.
    UiView.composing(String)Whether an input method holds uncommitted text in a field; leave keys to it while true.
    UiView.anchor(String)A UiAnchor on a mounted button or PICKER choice, for a popover or a dialog attached to it.
    UiView.withSecret(String, Consumer), UiView.clearSecret(String), UiView.replaceSecret(String, char[])Read a secret field's characters (erased after the callback), clear it, or set it without an edit event.
    UiView.registerContent(CustomContent)Fill a Nodes.Custom node with a component; see below.

    Reconciliation

    A view never mutates in place: the plugin builds the next tree and calls update. The kit matches the new tree to the mounted one by node id and kind, so a node that keeps its id and kind keeps what the user is doing in it, such as text being typed, focus and selection, while new ids are created and missing ones removed. Give nodes ids derived from the data they show (target + ".name"), not from their position, and keep them stable across updates. A field's value is what the plugin last set; the user's typing arrives as UiEvent.Edited and the plugin puts it in the next tree.

    Nodes

    KindNodes
    Text and statusNodes.Text (sixteen roles; the MONO roles mark data values such as hosts, paths and commands, drawn in the data face), Nodes.Icon, Nodes.StatusDot, Nodes.Chip, Nodes.Progress, Nodes.Strength, Nodes.Notice, Nodes.Properties, Nodes.Separator
    ControlsNodes.Button (PRIMARY, SECONDARY, GHOST, DESTRUCTIVE_GHOST, LINK), Nodes.MenuButton, Nodes.Field (TEXT, SEARCH, PORT, PATH, TEXTAREA, NUMBER), Nodes.Secret, Nodes.Choice (DROPDOWN, PICKER, EXCLUSIVE, SEARCHABLE, PREVIEWS, TABS), Nodes.PickerMenu, Nodes.Toggle, Nodes.Breadcrumbs
    CollectionsNodes.ItemList with ListItem rows (SINGLE, DOUBLE, COMPACT, ORDERED, RESULTS), Nodes.Table with Columns and TableRows, Nodes.Tree with TreeItems
    LayoutNodes.Stack (a Nodes.LayoutRole such as VERTICAL, INLINE or ACTIONS), Nodes.Card, Nodes.Section, Nodes.FormRow, Nodes.SettingRow, Nodes.Split, Nodes.Empty
    CompositionsNodes.Panel with its Nodes.Header, for tool windows; Nodes.Form (PROMPT, PROMPT_COMPACT, SHEET, FULL, SETTINGS, WINDOW), for dialogs, windows and pages
    CustomNodes.Custom, a slot for a registered component

    Every node has an id and a ControlState: visible, enabled, busy and error, the validation message the control shows. ControlState.READY is visible, enabled, not busy and without an error. Unless its submission is NONE, a form presses its single PRIMARY button on Enter, except when the focused control takes Enter itself (a field with a trailingAction, a secret with a submitAction, a PICKER choice, breadcrumbs being edited, or a list, table or tree row with an activate or Enter action), a popup is open, focus is in a text area, or the form or a visible, enabled control in it is busy or shows an error; Escape runs its cancel action.

    Events

    A control that runs something reports UiEvent.Action with the action key the plugin configured on it (a button's action, a list's activateAction), not its node id. The other events carry the id of the node they concern; item, option, row and column ids in them are local to that node.

    EventFrom
    UiEvent.ActionButtons, menu items, a field's Enter, Shift+Enter and Escape actions, a secret's copy and submit actions, a PICKER choice, picker menu rows, a list's, table's or tree's activate and key actions, a form's or stack's cancel action
    UiEvent.EditedFields, a searchable choice's free text, a picker menu's query, breadcrumbs being edited
    UiEvent.SelectedChoices, lists, tables, trees, a breadcrumb, the active row of a picker menu
    UiEvent.ToggledToggles; the event carries the toggle's node id and the new state
    UiEvent.ExpandedTree branches
    UiEvent.Removed, UiEvent.ReorderedORDERED lists
    UiEvent.SecretChangedSecret fields; it never carries the value
    UiEvent.ClickedA plain left click on a list, table or tree row, after its Selected
    UiEvent.SortedA table or tree column header

    The kit reports what the user asked for; the plugin decides. A toggle's checked is the state the plugin's tree last confirmed, and an ORDERED list's row goes when the plugin's next tree leaves it out.

    What a tree may not contain
